## Definitions

- [statement] PrintNinja’s dated USD benchmark is a 54-card poker deck with a printed tuck box on Blue Core 280 gsm: $2.69 per deck at 500 decks ($1,343 total) and $1.94 at 1,000 ($1,943 total). These are rounded displayed unit prices; use the quoted order totals for budgeting. This benchmark is not a quote for a larger game. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-02) — https://printninja.com/printing-prices/card-game-printing/ · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis · also: https://printninja.com/printing-products/card-game-printing/

## Structure and components

- [statement] The Game Crafter says to enter the total card count of a type across decks when building a quote; its example combines two decks of 20 poker cards as 40 cards. That quote omits stock components and cutting charges for certain custom-cut products, so those omissions need separate cost entries when applicable. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-01-22) — https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/23-game-costs · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis
- [statement] The Game Crafter labels its card components as priced by the sheet and warns that displayed component prices are configurable examples. The cached pricing table contains unresolved template expressions, so it does not establish a numeric card-sheet price or sheet capacity for this game. (low confidence) — https://www.thegamecrafter.com/make/pricing · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis
- [statement] The Game Crafter bases bulk discounts on games in an order, not sheets or components in one game. Discounts vary with components; a headline maximum is not a guaranteed discount. Its bulk-pricing page includes a per-copy handling fee starting at $0.89, falling to $0.79 at 500 copies and $0.69 at 1000 copies. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-06-01) — https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/84-bulk-pricing · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis

## How it works

- [statement] Modeling prescription derived from relevant-cost analysis: within a constant-cost volume range, ownership cost equals incremental fixed ownership cost plus variable manufacturing cost per accepted game times accepted games; outsourcing cost equals its fixed setup cost plus delivered cost per accepted game times accepted games. The ownership crossover is the fixed-cost difference divided by the per-game variable-cost saving. It exists at positive volume only when those differences permit it. No numeric crossover is established here. (low confidence) — https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/10-3-evaluate-and-determine-whether-to-make-or-buy-a-component · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis · also: https://extension.missouri.edu/publications/g648
- [statement] For ownership cost indifference, equate the relevant total cost of making with the relevant total cost of buying at the same output. Algebraically, when unit costs are constant, incremental fixed cost divided by per-unit savings gives the crossover quantity. A positive ownership payback requires a positive saving; neither a machine price nor an output speed alone determines that quantity. This is a model derivation, not an observed game-production break-even volume. (medium confidence) — https://lmscontent.embanet.com/Media/UND/ACCT509/ACCT509-w01-m01/index.html · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis · also: https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/10-3-evaluate-and-determine-whether-to-make-or-buy-a-component

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Recommended comparison convention: compute landed cost per accepted complete game as the relevant batch costs, including applicable freight, taxes, duties and rework, divided by accepted complete games. Record rejected or incomplete games separately. This is a proposed modeling convention derived from quote exclusions and the accounting text’s warning about quality-related replacements; no yield or failure rate is assumed. (medium confidence) — https://printninja.com/printing-prices/card-game-printing/ · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis · also: https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/10-3-evaluate-and-determine-whether-to-make-or-buy-a-component

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] PrintNinja’s price list includes printing, binding, packaging and electronic proofs, but excludes shipping, sales tax and duties. Its standard hard-copy card proof is a separate $450 one-time option with specified stock, finish and packaging limitations. Treat the published deck price as a manufacturing benchmark rather than landed cost. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-02) — https://printninja.com/printing-prices/card-game-printing/ · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis
- [statement] MU Extension’s costing method measures a full batch, including materials and packaging; labor runs through placing finished output into inventory. Apply this method to the finished game rather than printer page speed: obtain actual total labor hours and accepted complete games before assigning labor cost per game. This is a proposed application, not measured card-production performance. (low confidence) — https://extension.missouri.edu/publications/g648 · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis
- [statement] A single linear ownership crossover is conditional: MU Extension notes that volume discounts can lower variable unit costs while extra equipment or property raises fixed costs. Recompute at actual quote tiers and capacity changes rather than extending one unit price across every quantity. (medium confidence) — https://extension.missouri.edu/publications/g648 · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis · also: https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/84-bulk-pricing
- [statement] Ownership cost parity and business sales break-even answer different questions. MU Extension defines sales break-even units as fixed costs divided by selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit; that revenue-based formula must not be used as the equipment-versus-outsourcing crossover. (medium confidence) — https://extension.missouri.edu/publications/g648 · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis · also: https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/10-3-evaluate-and-determine-whether-to-make-or-buy-a-component, https://www.sba.gov/counseling/plan-your-business/, https://lmscontent.embanet.com/Media/UND/ACCT509/ACCT509-w01-m01/index.html
- [statement] PrintNinja gives different inclusion scopes for posted prices and order quotes: its price list excludes shipping, sales tax and duties, while its order guidance says USD quotes for USA delivery include taxes and duties. Preserve those attributed scopes and verify the actual quote rather than adding taxes or duties twice. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-02) — https://printninja.com/printing-prices/card-game-printing/ · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis · also: https://printninja.com/placing-an-order/
- [statement] The Game Crafter instructs quote users to enter the total number of cards of a given type for the whole game, including multiple decks. Count the complete game bill of materials rather than treating a stack as a whole game. (low confidence) — https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/23-game-costs · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis
- [statement] The Game Crafter says its custom-component quote excludes stock components. A complete game cost must add any applicable excluded parts instead of assuming the displayed custom-component total includes them. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-01-22) — https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/23-game-costs · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis
- [statement] Wiss recommends sensitivity analysis on maintenance assumptions, energy costs and utilization. For this game analysis, leave unmeasured operating inputs explicit and test alternative assumptions rather than inventing operating minutes, yield or equipment lifetime. (low confidence) — https://wiss.com/total-cost-of-ownership-manufacturing-equipment/ · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis

## Facts and statements

- [statement] MU Extension includes depreciation, repair and operating costs in equipment cost per hour and warns against counting the same expense again as a fixed cost. Equipment ownership may be allocated as fixed costs or through product operating costs, but those allocations must remain consistent. (low confidence) — https://extension.missouri.edu/publications/g648 · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis
- [statement] OpenStax’s make-or-buy analysis compares relevant costs: materials, labor and variable overhead differ between alternatives, while fixed costs that continue under either alternative do not determine the saving. Identify avoidable equipment and overhead costs before claiming an ownership advantage. (low confidence) — https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/10-3-evaluate-and-determine-whether-to-make-or-buy-a-component · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis
- [statement] Proposed landed-good-game accounting boundary: sum manufacturing, packaging, allocated setup, applicable inbound shipping, taxes and duties, and actual rework or replacement spending; divide by accepted complete games. Keep yield unknown until measured, and do not count replacement costs twice. This adapts batch input-output costing and the vendor’s explicit price exclusions; it is not a quoted landed price. (low confidence) — https://extension.missouri.edu/publications/g648 · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis · also: https://printninja.com/printing-prices/card-game-printing/, https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/10-3-evaluate-and-determine-whether-to-make-or-buy-a-component
- [statement] OpenStax says make-or-buy decisions also require quality, delivery, supplier-price and available-capacity assessment. A cheaper nominal per-unit figure alone does not establish an economically equivalent finished product. (low confidence) — https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/10-3-evaluate-and-determine-whether-to-make-or-buy-a-component · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis
- [statement] Wiss recommends modeling equipment ownership beyond acquisition: installation, maintenance and consumables, utilities, training and labor, downtime, and eventual disposal or residual value. This is a cost-category framework, not a measured cost or service-life estimate for card printing equipment. (low confidence) — https://wiss.com/total-cost-of-ownership-manufacturing-equipment/ · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis
- [statement] PrintNinja publishes a benchmark of US$2.69 per deck at 500 decks for a standard 54-card poker deck on Blue Core stock with a printed tuck box. It is a configuration-specific benchmark; it does not price the commissioned game. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-02) — https://printninja.com/printing-products/card-game-printing/ · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis · also: https://printninja.com/printing-prices/card-game-printing/
- [statement] PrintNinja’s published card-game price list excludes shipping, sales tax and duties. Those posted deck prices therefore do not by themselves establish a landed USD game cost. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-02) — https://printninja.com/printing-prices/card-game-printing/ · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis
- [statement] SBA recommends separating mixed costs into fixed and variable portions; its examples include repairs, indirect labor, fuel and power. Applying that classification prevents treating every operating expense as either a flat equipment charge or a constant per-game amount. (low confidence) — https://www.sba.gov/counseling/plan-your-business/ · keywords: Game manufacturing cost and break-even analysis
